The hard game against the softer net is still played, and there is an instance of it in the attack a hich is it MAU upon the seats of the three ladies returmal to the London Comity Council. Mr. lIHRLSFORD. Hove. nephew of Lord SALIST,ILT, and the rejected of Kennington, was beaten by Lady. 'SANDHURST in a contest f. :r the representation of Brixton on the London Comity Co .... cil. But it ROOMS that if Mr. Basesrono-1 fora could not storm the seat, be can undermine it ; he dial- • longed her qualification to sit, on the ground that she was .1 WM:MI, and, OD Saturday. in the Queen's Bench Division judgment was given in his • favour by Mr. .....TIP. STRPHRN. There is no question about women being entitled to vote at Comity Council elections, and, for that matter, to sit as Poor Law Guardians or members of School Boards ; lint, inasmuch as there is no express vision in the new Local Government Act giving them a title to election, it is ruled that they have no qualification. It is held that, as a County Coun- cil is constituted after the manner of a borough , emmeil, it agrees with it in their being no title ; for women to have seats ill the council. The decision therefore is that the votes given for Lady SANDHURST are s, many votes throws away, and Mr. %Hasson', Here iS titheui tip have been duly elected. Notice of appeal has been given, but we era not hopeful ,if the ruling being reversed ; and, if Lady Sasnntrawr is d.squuislitieui, Miss COBDEN and Miss CONS —tho latter an " alderman " by-the-by—are also disqualified. It would seem as if it were imneisible for Parliament to legislate without lomgling. In view of the fact that women have 11(1011 found so useful on School Boards and Boards of Guanlians, it is scarcely to be doubted that, if attention had been called to this ambiguity whilst the Local Government Bill was in progress it would have been remedied in the direction of perfecting the qualification of female burgesses. It is to be hoped that an amending • act will be immediately introduced, and carried through both Houses. It will not save the seats of the three Indies who ore not permitted to wear the ' laurels they have so well won but it will open the door on their behalf to the first vacancies that may wear. A CASE which was hoard at New- Khoo' t4m Petty Sessions, on Saturday, will serve its a warning to school teachers and school managers who aro in the habit of providing theatrical entertainments. Mr. F. BALL, schmil-teacherat Grin Board School, was brought before the magistrates for " causing stage plays to be perform.' in his schoolroom without a license," and some half-a-dozen boys and girls were summoned for " taking part in acting stage plays without a license." From the evidence given, there seems to have been no doubt as to a breach of the low having boon committed ; for two plsys were perforated —" Assurance" and 'The Three Graces." Mr. BALL, 88 Malinger of the entertainment, seems to have thought he had set hintself right as to the law by communicating with the publishers of the plays ; but Ile will now know that copyright is one thing, and a license to perform quite another. Indeed, if he had not been rather abroad as II FICIIOOI-tO.Wher, he would have ascertained that he was breaking the law, for, as a matter of fact, lie had had warn- ing that the performance of such plays, without license, was illegal. Perhaps ho thought he knew as much about the law as the police authorities, for ho remarked when cautioned that he should like to see the Act of Parliament. He ought to have seen that Act before he devoted the school to the performance which was given the other night, for studying Acts in a Police Court is pur- -1 suit of knowledge under difficulties. However, the I Bench were in a lenient mood ; they took motive into account, dismissing the case against the boys II and girls, and distaissi nn g the case against Mn, BALL on payment of ...eta It is a matter of course : to say that SIIIIREIRLEVIIIIIE WEIR Ilia 110 WIER MITI Ilk duty in taking proccedi nn gs. Baron de Worms says if you break down the sugar monopoly, you prevent speculators from artifically raising prices. Just so, blit Will his Sugar Convention have this effect 9 From the way the price of sugar has gone up of late, it d.ms not look very mach like it. The country is being bamboozled on the question. Bring the Conven- timi into operation, and the price of sugar will go higher still, and that is why English sugar mer- chants like it. They want to grow rich at the expense of the pair the millions of lame who use sugar as daily food.

But when did the Tories go to the poll us n "split' I party ? They can always teach the Liberals a . lesson as to "piecing up." At Rochester, on Tuesday, there was a fair awl square tight—it was a contest between Tory and Liberal ; mid the Liberal won by what, for Roches- ter, is the substantial majority of 7.1. Birmingham left things as they were so far as political repre- tentati ~,, is concerned ; but the result at Roches- ter is a distinct Liberal gain. Tim Tory poll on Tuesday showed a decline of 20, while the Liberal vote has risen 302. There is only one reasonable explanation of such a change, and that is that the coontry is growing day by day isore and more in favour of Rome Rule.

div.head: ALLEGED LIBEL ON MR. BRENNER, M.P.
div.p: ALLEGED LIBEL ON MR. BRENNER, M.P.

The Press Association learnt that Mr. .1. T. Brunner, Ml'., has instructed Messrs. Lewis and Lewis to commence an action for libel against Mr. IL Champion, the well known Socialist. The state- ments impugned appeared in a scree of articles in the defendant's paper, "The Labour Elector," in which Mr. Brunner was accused of sweating employes at Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co's Alkali Works, Winnington and Sandbach, Cheshire, and with culpable carelessness resulting in loss of life and personal injury to a large number of work- people. Sir Charles Russell, Mr. Finlay and Mr. Asquith have been retained as Mr. Brunner's counsel.

Blessed or cursed, whichever you like to call it, with a mind capable of extensive vision, I have been so bewildered and perplexed by the sorry spectacle pre- sented by humanity in its world-wide aspect as to for- I get the quaint little town in which, for the present at 1 any rate,my dailylot is east. But, afterall, the problems of a town are substantially the same as the problems of a world; the incidentals are different, the essentials are the same. Warrington is a small city, a small nation, a world;await and the difficulties of life confront us here if anywhere.

div.head: HEAVY HATES.
div.p: HEAVY HATES.

" GRANDMOTHERLY LEGISLATION." Sir.—A letter in your iASUP. signed " Thomas Hardy, Runcorn," seems to be aunts' at mine of the previous week, under theabove title; and for rich wrong-headed- nets it beats anything I ever saw in print. Indeed, were It not for its success in proving " flow not to do it," it would not be worth the Ink slung upon it,to say nothing of the serious brain-perturbation that it carnes On its very face. Ily your leave, I will point out a few—but by no means all—of the ludicrous twistings I.f Thomas Hardy's mind, which will prove to a nteety how ill- advised he was to sign his name, and to publish his folly, although he carps at toe for noq signing time, I Idol not object to "my V7llO and family copying my example," but I showed how probable it was that they would dons. 2 : I nevar mid anything about" the Liquor Traffic being either gotsl or bad," though I take leave to say that it is as good as any other, if properly conducted, 3: I never mid it WOO" not earned on openly and freely like other usefid trw444 i" Is; I know it is, and rightly to. 4 I never mid it "Is at war with virtue and morality," for I don't believe it is ; and I take leave to My that the individuals who preach such ridiculous rublmh are fanatics of the deepest dye, who work on theory only; and who will, of mimeo, ho the imtruments in the devil's hands for encouraging private drinking. This "Thomas Hardy "can't or wont (the latter most probably) see that, if lie shuts up the Public HouSee on Sundays, private drinking must inevitably follow. In , the course of my business, I have, unforttmatelv, been often compelled to spend the Sunday in towns where the Sunday Closing Act is in force ; and I my, with aluoltite truth, that I have seen more drunkards in the strmts of those towns and heard more unseemly IIOiSCS in the houses on the Sabbath, than in any place where there is no prohibition. So much for actual experience as against the wire-dr:l'am them ies of the famtical " faddists." These are the men who '• would ponder to the people ;" , and in spite td your mrtaspondent's dogmatic dictum, it will, whilst not doing either" %Index "or anybody else any good, serve to i1.61t `4 Thomas Hardy," and such as he, in doing incaleadable mischief, and taming innunier- able private houses, into secret drinking chop.! "The Pets in favour of Sunday Closing are no few, and the 'thrones so plentiful and false, that they have been eontroverted thousands of times; but to convince a teetotal bigot is harder than to drive a joke into a Highlander's bead. With regard to my " stomach," I only wish it was stronger than my brains, and I speak feelingly. That I nmsider a glass of good beer, or goo I wine, or ewn good whisky, as of God's gifts, is no proof that I am ignorant, but indeed i 4 very much the other way, and I will not believe "Thomas Hardy " is fool mmugh to think otherwise, however, he may preach. That lam a " fossil Tiny" is also one of his fade; and one of my friends to whom I showed this letter, when he Came this hardy "fact." asked " if " I knew this— " Jerusalem PO. Scribbler !" The " Fanatiml Faddists" have not succinct...l in anything emmpt making them- selves laughing-stocks and pronounced tneddlers of the very worst type; and whilst I to thoroughly enjoy their discomfiture lam FlOl. atupid unto emigrate, either 1,, Scotia nd, Wiles. on the State of Maine, where I should go unquestionable " further and fare worse," bemuse of these 'AIM grand-motherly efforts at being good. And finally. I assert, that the Irian who believes that closing puhlie•houses on Sundays will not encourage private drinking to the debauching of thousands of quiet homes, and who believm that people min be made ~00tsl by Act of Parliatnent, inn man whom Colnoy Hatch would reject as hopeless, and Bedlam steadfastly refuse to admit, as too dangerous. Earlsstown, 17th April, 1889,

div.head: SUICIDE OF A LOVER.
div.p: SUICIDE OF A LOVER.

An inquest has heist held at Great Cornard, Suffolk, on the body of John Shave, aged twenty-one, who conimitted suicide IT drowning himself in the river Stour. He had been courting a young woman named Betty Bruce, who gave evidence. She said they had been engaged for eighteen months, and had never had a ends word in all that thin.. Tier lover Anffered much with his back, having strained it fifteen months ago when lifting a piece of iron, and at times he was very quiet, but be (lid not take a very low-spirited view of the matter. He woo with her on Friday evening, and on Saturday night she received die following letter fmm him, written in pencil ffdurday evening. My darling.—When you read this letter I shall be in another land far away. I have not the conscience to meet you again on earth, so I have done awn y with myself ; but, my own dear girl, I do not want you to fret at all about me. for lam not worth it. loin exceedingly sorry to think I hurt your feelings last night ; the Lord knows it. You asked mot° forgive you ; but it was me that wanted forgiveness, but I was ashanevl to ask you. What few thing« you have of mine k.(-1( and say nothing about them. The little money you have of mint. spend 1 on yourself. I beg of you not to let this tnnable you, 1 fort do not know what to do with myself, and this is what I have chosen. Love to mother. I eanmd ask you to accept my love, font am not worthy of it. My darling, I wish you good-bye, and God bless you. P.:". —lf you want Sc, find nip I shall be down by Lady's Bridge."—Mks Bruce, continuing, said she did dot know what the deceased meant in his letter by " hurting her feeling," Ile had comolained abont being chaffed by Site daughter of the landlord of the house where he lodged, but the witness was not jealous of her as she knew the deceased did not think anything of the girl.— The constable who examined the body said he found under a waistbelt, next the shirt of the delyased, a por- trait of Miss Bruce.—A verdict M.OO returned that the deceased drownal I ' self whilst in a temporary state of insanity.—A very affecting scene took place in the yard at the rear of the inn where the inqiiest was held, when Miss Bruce took • last Vieß of Iva dead lover. She embraced the corpse, kissing it passionately.

It was suggestesl that Mr. Lowe, estate Rout and secountant, stead,' take the post, having a centrW office, and being at liberty to taLe sulagriptions, or attend to other business at any time, and to my mind that seems so if some of the duke work required doing when Mr. Howard should be attending to his Corporate duties. Sir,—l was glad to we from your paper the other week, that we are to get some little direct benefit from the accumulation of funds in connection with the Gas Works It is no bad thing that £BOO or £7OO a year are to be caws' to the Corporation by reducing the charges for the street lamps, but that does not touch the question of what is to be done with the £20,000., which was stated to have accumulated sines: the purchase of the Ow Works by the Corporation. I should like to ask why don't one TOWn Councillors take the matter up and let us have a settlement in one way or the other? las a ratepayer tag to thank Couneil/or Voisey for haring taken no nuteli trisuble to go into accounts to bring to light the facts as to the funds in hand. and 8110111li he glad if he, ss-, for that matter, any other Councillor, %mad follow the matter up by bringing forward some definite scheme for disposing of the balance. It seems to roe that the price to the consumer ought to be reduced, and that the ratepayers tnight to some extent have the benefit of the balance in reduced rates. Ono or both souses sought certainly to he taken, and the ..ner it is done thss better.—Yours, he., Warrington. April 113th, 1889.

...... Mr. 6.--Mais-si..sr, curator and librarian of the War- rington Museum, next mad a paper on •. some obsolete modes of punishment," illustrated by the exhibition of the atoeka, scold's bridle, mantrap, spring gun, and gibbet irons.

Of all the instruments of punishment, he said, the best known were tlie stocks. They might take ai a type the example nearmt at hand. The Orappenhall stock.s inn. Sated, firstly, of two square posts of stone standing some yard and a half apart, and having a groove or slot cut in that side of each which faosl inwards. In the grooves were held a pair of thick boards standing on olge—the one on the other—the lower board being fixed, whilst the lower one slid inn the grooves it ndcould be fastened down, when in um, with a padlock. Those were the "jaws" of the stocks. Through the two hoards at their junction two pain of round holes were cut—half inn the upper, half in the lowerboard—of such a simthat when a manfi ankles were laid in Owns and the upper jaw shut down the prisoner would be unahle to withdraw his feet. A neat was provident for the prisoner, upon nn-hich he sat with his legs stuck straight out in front ; but at Orappenhall, as usually elsewhere, the seat was now wanting. Subject to slight variations, that VIM the common form of the stocks, and inn position tine pair at Grappenliall were equally typical. One of the posts there was carefully renewed mine 15 years ago, but the mat was not replaced ; and when the village street was last repaired, the level of the ground was raised an as partially to bury the lower jaw of the stocks, and within the last few weeks One beginning of the end has come in the total disappearance of the upper jaw.

The stocks at LyMni,-Widcli.;b7ind in so prominent a position at the foot of the steps of the villiage cross, were fastened up, but there the "spiking" had evislently lit4,n done at a recent date, and the removal of two iron wedges was all that was necessary to restore the stocks to a " usable " comlition. That to Ant was important as indicating a genuine specimen. The jaws of the Lymrn , stocks were apparently of coictiderable age. They were weathemd away to about half their original thick/Ims, and had been Arengthened at various times with iron plates. Both at High Leigh and Lyn= the posts were of stone, and the seat was wanting at each place.

The purposes feir-wiiiWthe—nt;;Citt--tVere used were et two kinds. Firstly, there were those offenders for whom the punishment was prescribed in the statutes, chief of whom were runaway labourers, drunkards, and Sabbath- breakers. Secondly, the stocks being always at hand, and applicable with little trouble or expense, they wen. frequently adopted as o mild alternative to the line or imprisonment which, was the legal due of any minor offender. The stocks would thusbe likely to become, and there in little doubt did become, an imtrument of manorial and municipal discipline of the most effective kind, even where that wits not the original Object of their erection.

That the resignation of Mr. Bradshaw from the Widnes School Board severs another link in the chain of the pa.st, and with Mr. Timmis the rate- mem will regret the cause of his retirement. Mr. Bradshaw has been a member of the Board since its formation twelve years ago, and his colleagues have testified their confidence by placing him in every position of trust in their power. The town has lost a conscientious painstaking representative. That it is fitting that one of the chief men in the community should be at the head of our local affairs, and the re-election of Mr. Gossage to the position of Chairman of the LOCIII Board meets with universal approval. Mr. Goasage has now presided over the deliberations of the Local Board for ten consecutive years !
